messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always been a man who moved with purpose, his long legs eating up the distance as he danced across the stage. But that was before the accident, before the sound of screeching tires and crunching metal became etched in his mind like a scar. It had been two years since the motor vehicle collision that nearly took his life, but for Kofi, time seemed to have frozen. As he lay in the hospital bed, Kofi couldn't shake the feeling that something was off. He remembered fragments of the accident - the smell of smoke, the sound of sirens - but the rest was a jumbled mess. He tried to piece together what had happened, but his mind felt like a puzzle with missing pieces. This sense of incompleteness only added to his growing unease; he couldn't trust that he would ever be able to recall the truth. As Kofi began to recover physically, he found himself increasingly withdrawn. He stopped going out, afraid of being in public spaces where anything could happen. He avoided seeing people he had socialized with before the accident, unable to bear their questions or sympathetic gazes. Even thinking about the therapy sessions he knew he needed felt like too much; he couldn't bring himself to confront the memories that lingered just beneath the surface. Kofi's self-doubt had taken root early on. He questioned whether he would ever be able to trust his body again, whether he was truly safe even in his own home. The people and institutions that were supposed to protect him - the police, the hospital staff - seemed to have failed him, leaving him feeling vulnerable and alone. As a result, Kofi became hyper-vigilant, always on the lookout for potential threats. He felt safest with his back against a wall, where he could see everything happening around him. Delays or unexpected noises sent his heart racing; he was convinced that something bad was lurking just out of sight. Kofi's memories of the accident remained frustratingly incomplete, and this only added to his sense of unease. He felt like he was stuck in a never-ending loop, unable to move forward because he couldn't shake the feeling that he was missing something crucial. This uncertainty fueled his negative appraisals - he couldn't trust himself or anyone else. As Kofi struggled to come to terms with what had happened, his avoidance behaviors became more entrenched. He stopped dancing altogether, afraid of putting himself in a situation where he might get hurt again. His isolation deepened; he barely left the house, unable to bear the thought of facing the world outside. It was only when Kofi's granddaughter began to ask why "Papa" wasn't coming to visit anymore that he realized how much his life had shrunk. He knew he needed help, but the thought of seeking therapy filled him with dread - what if they uncovered memories he couldn't handle? What if he wasn't strong enough to face the truth? Kofi's story is one of a man trapped in a cycle of fear and self-doubt, unable to escape the shadow of his traumatic experience. His maladaptive strategies have become a way of life, but at what cost? As he sits in his darkened living room, surrounded by memories of a life once lived, Kofi wonders if it's too late to find a way back to the light.
